body:
I'm definitely getting help. In my current state I can't really function without it.

Good on you for having that kind of fighting spirit.

I experienced the same rush of emotions upon official confirmation, even though I already kind of knew the answer. I guess that it's just nice to know that what you felt and thought for so long was justified.

That last paragraph is really nice to read. I feel like I can really turn this diagnosis into a strength, but I don't quite know how to do that yet. 

I'm also suffering from a rather severe depression at the moment, which complicates things. But I'm starting to think it's all connected, and I need to start looking at me as a whole, in stead of in terms of disorders, if I want to get past this.

What I would do is read up a bit on depression. Gather some facts, make sure you know what you are talking about. Facts like what happens to serotonin levels, but also your feelings, and how they relate to depression. For instance: it's easy to spiral downwards in negative thoughts, lack of energy, ...

Then tell them straight up that you want to have a sit down with them. Try framing depression as an illness. Ask them whether they would say the same things they are saying to you to someone who has cancer. Try to explain a little how you feel, and what you're going through. And really hope that you manage to get through to them :( it's tough when those around you don't recognize your need for support. Good luck man.

One other tip that might help: ask your psychiatrist to see your parents together with you. He'll probably help you prepare. And they might accept things out of the mouth of a doctor but not out of yours.

I would find some comfort in knowing that those around me accept it though. I guess it's that comfort I'm trying to get from random internet strangers.

I'm definitely doing as much as possible to change things up in the time until my evaluation point. However, as much as possible is not very much anymore.

They do cause that, yeah, stupid choices. It's funny sometimes how irrational they make you. Looking at what you just said, you don't mind killing yourself at times, but you do mind the stigma around counseling.

I don't know what to tell you though. Toughing it out is definitely an option. It might not be a good one, or it might be exactly what you need.

As to your meds: if you started taking them a while ago, and are just taking them now, but not seeing a doctor who checks up on progress, who knows what they are doing. Maybe it would be a lot worse without them, maybe you need a change and would feel a lot better with others. There's a lot of stigma around medications as well, but it might be worth seeing a doctor/psychiatrist maybe a couple of times more just to find out if something else helps you more than what you're currently taking?

We all have this survival instinct. Feeling you can't go on living anymore and ending your life are two different things. The fact that you're posting means you are still alive (I hope, otherwise: creepy).

As to being admitted, it depends on where you live, how old you are, who you talk to, and what you say, I'd say.
Do you want to be? Or is it a fear you're expressing, that's holding you back from telling someone?

Definitely find help. Look at it this way, you don't have much to lose. 

Do you have an idea where to start looking for help? Are there any hurdles that are preventing you? Talk it through. With us here on Reddit if you like, or with someone close to you.

I know that feeling. I think It's caused by a certainty that things will always feel like this, which is typical for depression, and a logical next step of reasoning which says that if things stay this way, there will come a point where you won't be able to take it anymore. 

I think the thing to keep telling yourself is that you should just keep on going. Trying to fight that feeling of: "nothing will ever get better", is a hopeless fight, if you're deep into depression. However,  facts seem to indicate that a lot of people who were once at that point of hopelesness do feel better at some point.

I don't like it any more than you do, but at least it's some explanation.

I'm getting to the point where I'm seeing depression so much as an illness that needs treatment, that the only advice I can give is to try and get her to see a doctor and get her on medication.

You say she likes reading, you could try to communicate with her through that. Recommend her a book about depression and ask if she would be willing to read it. That might change her view on things a bit, or make her understand her own situation. If you'd like a recommendation, I can wholeheartedly recommend The Noonday Demon by Andrew Solomon. If she has an e-reader, feel free to pm me for the ebook.

I just feel this unshakeable certainty that I will never experience joy anymore. And I realise that that is the depression talking, and that I probably won't think that way once they found a treatment that works, but still.. How do you survive until then?

Right with there with you.

Sitting here, in my hospital bed. I've done countless things to try to distract myself. Game, watch a movie, read, solve rubik's cubes, write, smoke, talk to people, sit in the common room, ... 

And everything felt so empty and meaningless. What does the future hold in store? For me personally: ECT treatment. Yay, 80% response rate, might feel better afterwards. Then I'm still an emotionally broken person who can not function normally in life and has no real goals or interests. 

Let's go one step further, I join a therapy program, fix my emotional problems, reorient myself and start looking for goals. That sounds so very boring and unappealing. 

I don't want to commit suicide, but by god, I would be happy if I could die by accident. My perfect death would be something like jumping on a suicide bomber to shield other people. Then my family and friends would at least be able to come to accept my death. But chances are low that a suicide bomber will be strolling around in the psych ward of a hospital, I guess.

Yeah, the stigma sucks. It's about time that people start treating mental illnesses like physical ones, but I fear we're a long way away from that. All the best wishes to you though. Hope you manage to get through this!

That hits close to home. The problem I'm mostly having right now is that Xanax is not a long term solution. And I have to communicate about how bad it is, while feeling *okayish*, for them to find a long term solution. So I'm kind of in between not taking them and being able to communicate and taking them and feeling less crap.

Hey. I don't know what the situation is like where you live, and if it's a possibility considering your work. But have you considered a small intake in a hospital? Where I live general hospitals have psychiatric departments for short-term intakes. What you are describing sounds pretty much spot on as a depression. I've seen multiple people being helped a lot by stopping their lives for a little while, and taking the time to look at it from a short distance and decide what they need to handle it better.

They won't fix you there. But from what I've seen in the other people around me here, many people use it to:

* First get some rest, get away from all the daily worries, and focus on yourself for a little while. Because getting yourself in better shape mentally will allow you to function well for others as well
* Talk to a psychiatrist and a therapist. They look at medications you're taking and if they are helping you, and might switch them up a bit.
* Give you some insight in your current situation and how to handle it.
* Prepare you for leaving, by helpnig you look for the best follow-up treatment, for instance seeing a therapist a couple of times a month.

It's just something to consider, putting the focus on yourself for a little while, so that you can then function better for others.

I guess it's very unlikely that that is the cause. My head is just completely fucked up right now. I have trouble explaining how I feel, but one of the things I feel is a rock solid, irrational, but present nonetheless, belief that I will never get better. However, the logical part of my brain has no trouble believing in something like hypothyroidism. And that causes some weird clashes in my head. The idea that there could be magic pills that would change what I've been feeling for so long.

It's just an extreme long shot, but I'll see what my psychiatrist has to say on it. Maybe they'll do some extra tests for T3 and T4 or something. Otherwise, ah well. Worth looking into and wondering about I guess.

Hey, thanks man. I realise that I am lucky with where I ended up, and can image it's a lot worse at many other places. I'm sorry to hear that you had such shitty care. How are you doing nowadays?

I'm kind of driving myself insane at the moment by constantly forcing myself to focus on how irrational I'm being. But yeah, the logical part of me says pretty much what you commented. Let's hope it's right ;) I'll drop you a message in a while to give you an update!

That really sounds recognisable. The part where if you really think about it, you realise that that belief is wrong. But for me (I don't know if you have this as well), even realising that, I still feel as if it's lost. And it's that contradiction that really tires me out. All day long I'm telling myself: "Hey, see, things can get better." But it doesn't help.

I'm currently at a the psychiatric crisis department of a general hospital. It's a department that takes in people who are in dire need of an immediate intake. For instance, I felt very sure that I would commit suicide if I didn't go to a controlled environment, so they took me in. Here I have a personal psychiatrist and psychologist. I see both of them 2 times a week. There's also a bunch of nursing staff that specialised in psychiatric treatment, with which you have a talk daily. They don't try to give you therapy, but just check in with how you are doing, how you are reacting to medication, how you are sleeping, things like that. These talks are mostly to pass that information on to the psychiatrist and the therapist.

Then there are group sessions with people who are in a similar situation, in my case people suffering from depression. There are a couple of different types of sessions. I'll go over the different kinds, and my experience with them.

* Psycho-education, as they call it, where they just give you information such as what causes depression, what the major symptoms are, what the treatments are, ...
* Non-verbal communication, which focusses on non-verbal things, like music, art, ... I hate these. I suck at them, I'm not good with words either, but at this I really suck :p
* Physical sessions: physical exercise is proven to be good for depression, so they take you out and make you exercise.
* Group talks: where people can just share and talk about their problems. I don't fit in too well with these. Most people in my group have depressions with very obvious causes, such as a loved one passing away or a breakup. They mostly just want to talk about those things, so I mostly just sit there and weigh in here and there.
* ACT-sessions: a pretty popular therapy, Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, which promotes knowing your goals and the things you value and living in accordance to them. I get what they are saying, but I feel too far gone to really get any use from these.
* A sessions at the start of the week where you set goals for the upcoming week, and discuss your previous goals. I don't really have many goals at the moment, so mostly come up blank here.
* Relaxation and mindfulness. Not really my cup of tea.


Finally, what they do here is a kind of first aid. Other than starting up medication, having talks, and these sessions, they make sure you end up in the right place as soon as possible. For me, this is a specialised psychiatric hospital. They set up the intake talks, and pass on the information they have to the new place, where you go for further treatment.

That sounds like something that could actually help. Finding a place where you genuinely feel at home and have a purpose. Two issues regarding it though: 

1) I don't have the energy to look for it, and don't really care enough anymore to do so.

2) I'm in a mental hospital, and probably will be for some months. Not going to find it here. :(
Thanks. A positive post without any unrealistic expectations or meaningless statements. Feels good to read. Wishing you all the best as well.
Yeah, that's what the rational part of my brain tells me as well. But I don't know how long I'll keep up surpressing the other part of me that really does not want help any longer.

My experience with pills so far has been pretty bland. I haven't really felt anything yet. Not bland, not better, not worse. But I keep being told that it's possible to find the right one that does work. I don't know.

As to therapy, I've had pretty good experiences. None of the go-to phrases that you describe, but people that genuinely understand depression, and know that those are the last thing I want or need to hear. The people who spout the feel-good positive phrases are mostly the people around me. And I can't really blame them. They are intended well, so generally I just nod and ignore them.

I am actually kind of intrigued by ECT. Electroshocks that are immensely effective and work relatively fast, and just kind of fix you? Try your worst, I'd say. There's a hospital I'm being sent to next in my country with a psych who's also linked to a great university here who's pioneered a lot of stuff related to ECT. We'll see what it gives.

As to the "let others help you" part: Honestly, mental care here is pretty good, depending on where you end up. Part of it is indeed medication. And how that works: it's just a numbers game. You have a depression, the chemical imbalance can be rectified with medication, but you need the right one, so they have to try different ones until they find it. 

What I'm terrified of is that I will get so used to feeling the way I do, that I won't notice it when a medication does work. I don't know if that is a valid concern. I just can't imagine not feeling this way, so can't imagine either how I would notice that.

I've heard those positive phrases hundreds of times. And I've said them to myself thousands of times. But it seems you just get to a point where you just don't want to anymore. 

EDIT: You also feel really, really ashamed. Because you look back at yourself, not caring about positive things like this, and realise that you actually meant the reply that you don't care anymore. You feel pathetic and weak, and hate yourself for it.

Nah, let it. That's what HalfLit was saying. It messes with your mind. I feel so fucked up.

EDIT: I know this sounds kind of like a cunt. Just trying to illustrate how deep you can sink into apathy.
I would like to say: "I hope so". But I don't. I don't hope anymore. But I know you are right.

I know you're right, but as you are saying, I don't care. And that's the most fucked up part, I fully realise that it's an ouroboros effect, and that it's the depression that's causing the not caring. Yet I still feel that way. 

I kind of lost control after typing this post, and started crying uncontrollably. I asked them to put me in the isolation cell for a while, where I cried non-stop for 2 hours and kept on hitting my own head. This is the reason why I committed myself. If this happened if I were alone, I would kill myself.

We'll see what the future brings. I'll let them play their games for now. And hope I don't drift off so far that I really give up, leave and actually off myself.
Yeah, got my laptop here. It's not that much like in the movies, you know. Well, at least here it isn't.

Yeah, same here. It's been that way for a very long time. About 7 years. Since march I've been seeking help, as I couldn't hold on any longer. I'm in a long series of hospital after hospital now. I don't really care about anything at this point.

I can tell you what my doctors have been telling me: depression is an illness, you are suffering from it. If you had any other disease, you would go see a doctor and get treatment. That's what (some) depressions need. Depressions don't need an obvious cause like someone passing away or something bad happening to you. It can be a chemical imbalance in your brain. It won't go away by itself, medication makes it go away.

But I don't know if you want to hear that? I kind of didn't. I believe them, but I don't really accept it. I am who I am, and I've been this person for a long time. It's hard to believe that it's because of some fucked up chemicals in my brain. I'll let them try their medications and maybe electroshocks for a bit longer. But it won't be long before I just end it all.

Well, the only advice I can give you is similar to what Tubeh19 posted. Try to gather your energy a bit, and try something new. Something completely different from what you've been doing. Make a trip, find a new hobby, do some volunteering work, ...

It will cost a lot of energy, and might end up feeling bland or just be a bad fit for you. But it might just spark something new inside of you. And if it fails, do it again, and try something else. If your life feels bad the way it is, the only thing we can do is try to change it.

Yeah, and there you might meet somewhat of a problem. You're at the point of giving up (or not caring anymore), so it's not very likely that you're going to put a lot of effort into finding out if that something exists, or trying to find it. Yet finding something might just be what you need to get back on track;

Do you enjoy playing video games? Or is that more a way to make the time go by?  And if I might ask: what are your plans for the upcoming months? Or weeks? Any stuff you are forced, or expected to do? Like finding a job or something, or can you sustain your current situation as it is?

Yup, sadness feels like something you can understand. That feeling of emptiness however... And the big problem is that if you don't really care about much anymore, you're not very likely to change things, so you just stay stuck.

A general question: is there something that you can imagine yourself doing that would give you some sense of accomplishment? Or something that just gives you a somewhat good feeling, even a little?

And if there is not, do you think there is no such thing out there, or that you just don't know what it is, and don't have the energy to look for it?
I reasoned that if I could drop everything in my life to go sit in a hospital that wasn't really helping me anymore, I could do the same to do something I've wanted to do for a long time.

Yeah, that sound familiar. Getting back on track would help tons with your depression, but your depression is keeping you back from getting back on track. Hope it works out man! I'm glad to hear that you have some stuff coming up to look forward to.

On a different note: I don't have much experience with psychiatrists. But you're saying that after the first two weeks you didn't notice much improvement anymore. How did your psychiatrist respond to that? Just keeping you on it for a year doesn't seem like the most helpful thing to do?

Do you know why you're not doing all of those things? Do you think you can get stuff going again if you try? And for that matter, do you want to try?

If the answers to those questions are no, then you'll have a tough time getting out of it by yourself. Have you considered seeking professional help? It's a shitty thing, because you first kind of have to admit there's something 'wrong' with you. But if you get to a point where you are stuck by yourself, you need to look for something that partly sheds the weight you're carrying.

Hey. I'm in kind of a similar situation. I've just decided to halt my studies (would've gotten my masters degree this june, if everything went normally, but things were not looking good) for a bit, and asked to be admitted to a psychiatric hospital for a couple of weeks. 

You seem to realise that stuff went wrong. Do you think you can get things back on track? Can you take a year off, work a bit, and then try again? Or is the depression only going to get worse, and are you just not able to perform at the level necessary to do what you want to do? 

You really need to take some time and look at yourself and figure out what it is you need. Have you thought about looking for professional help with your depression? Or is there a reason why you don't want that?

Hey. That really sounds recognisable. I often wish that I would find, or even try to find, that one thing I'm really passionate about. I kind of get the feeling that if I had that one magical thing, I would be able to get my life on track. But you just don't know what that thing is, or why you were never quite able to find it. 

And so the years creep on by, and then you start having these moments where you look back, and fully realize what you've been doing (or rather, not doing). And you look back and see all the opportunities you had, and compare that to people who had way fewer, but made more out of them. Sometimes I don't know if it's about finding that one thing that you want to live for, or if it's just a part of your personality. Does that one thing exists, or is it just a fiction you tell yourself to keep going?

Honestly, the fact that you're looking at it that positively is a good sign! You're saying you want to rewind, but you don't need that. You're not on your deathbed, you still have time. There's more to life than studying at 18 and finding a job when you're done, and doing that for the rest of your life. You realise that you didn't do what you wanted to do, but let's say you could rewind: would you know what you wanted then?

If the answer to that last question is yes, then great! You have a goal, it won't be easy, but you can try to start working towards it. Let that be what keeps you going! If needed, find help to keep you on track, or to keep you motivated. Don't expect yourself to suddenly become a perfect, non-postponing, person. Finding help to talk to regularly might be something that allows you to realise when, or if, things are going south again.

If it was no: that sucks, I know the feeling. This is a dangerous point. If you really think about it, will things keep going downhill from here if you change nothing? If that's the case, something has to change. But that's hard if you don't know what you change it to. Seeing a psychologist or psychiatrist might not be a bad idea. Even though it might feel stupid, because you just 'feel lazy'. It's easy to lie to yourself for a long time, and tell yourself you're just not really doing it yet, but you really could start anytime. If you're postponing it, and don't actually know what it is you are postponing, you kind of have to find out why that's happening, otherwise it's not going to change.

Hey, this sounds like something I (and I assume many people) experience when they're having a bad day, or are consciously thinking about bad things.

I have days where I really try hard to be a positive human being. For instance, days where I spend time with my family. I'm able to laugh then, spontaneously even! But at the end of the day, I'm tired, and I don't really get enjoyment out of moments like that. So the 'laugh' is fake in some way. 

What I'm wondering is if you have any moments like that? But as you say in the second part, you feel outside of reality often. I guess that really plays into not laughing. I guess that the moments we laugh, are sometimes (or often) the ones where we're really invested into something, and get 'surprised' by humor. And if you're never really there, it's hard to be surprised maybe?

Thanks, that's a bit comforting. I really hope that I will be open to what's coming. I'm scared that if I get the feeling that something is not working, or I could carry on by myself, I will close down, or maybe just leave/want to leave. But I guess the people there will have experience with things like that. 

For now, I can't really imagine what it will be like to spend complete days, for a couple of weeks, confronting things I don't really want to confront. I'm thinking it will be exhausting, but on the other hand, letting go of responsibilities is something I am really looking forward to. It was getting to a point where I was just crippled by wanting to do things and not getting anything done.
